definition.title: What is a venture architect?
definition.introduction: A venture architect is the person accountable for the design of a new business before it exists, and for the integrity of that design through its first build.

sections.title: The architect of record
paragraphs: I use the word architect in its building sense: one person working for the owner, accountable for how the parts fit together. The design comes before the build, the work is checked against it, and the engagement ends when the handover is complete.

A new business may have a strategist who wrote the case, a technical lead who chose the stack, lawyers who shaped the entity and a sponsor who approved the budget. Each has a part. The venture architect holds the whole.

sections.title: The decisions
paragraphs: The design comes down to a small set of connected decisions: what the business sells, what it prices in, what each unit costs to deliver, what it buys or builds, what it inherits, who governs it and how it is funded.

These decisions sit in three layers: commercial, technical and institutional. Price may be set by one person and cost by another. The relationship with a parent may be negotiated by lawyers and lived by the product team. The joints are the architect's territory.
Each decision needs a record: the choice, the alternatives rejected, the reasons and the evidence that would cause us to change it.

sections.title: Why AI changes the design
paragraphs: In an AI-native business, the architecture is the business model. Models, routing and human review affect the cost and quality of delivery. The choice between a system that does the work and one that helps a person do it affects the offer and the price.
These are business decisions made in technical language. They need to be made together, before the first build commits the venture to them.

sections.title: One accountable seat
paragraphs: The venture architect works for the owner and brings no build team to sell. That independence matters when the evidence says to stop.
The role holds design authority across all three layers. It requires someone who has held the technical seat in a new business and lived with business design decisions as a founder.

sections.title: Design, prove, hand over
paragraphs: In design, I make the decisions with the sponsor and founders. I write down the alternatives and the conditions for stopping before anyone is invested in the answer.
In prove, I hold the technical seat while the first version reaches committed customers. I report cost and quality at each gate so capital is released against evidence.

In handover, I hire the permanent technical lead and leave on the date written into the letter at the start. A fixed date gives the engagement a clear purpose: make the team capable of running what we designed.

sections.title: Where the practice comes from
paragraphs: My work has moved from applications to enterprises to whole ventures. During nine years at McKinsey, I served as CTO of North America's first large-scale digital business build, stood up next to an industrial parent.

I have built AI systems hands-on since 2021, written my own method for standing up an AI-native venture next to a PE-backed services firm, and run two ventures of my own. The work keeps the design accountable to what it costs to live with.

items.question: Is this a fractional CTO?
answer: The technical seat is part of the engagement. The scope is the design of the whole business: what it sells, what it costs to deliver, who governs it and when it stops. I hold the technical seat only until the design is proven and a permanent lead is in place.

items.question: How does this relate to a venture studio?
answer: My role is to work for the owner as an independent design authority. I bring no build team to sell. If a studio or engineering team is part of the build, the same design decisions, evidence gates and stopping conditions still apply.

items.question: We already have a strategy firm. Where do you fit?
answer: I work alongside advisory firms. My focus is the design decisions that connect the business case to a working system, and accountability through the handover to a permanent technical lead.

items.question: Can you work with the team we already have?
answer: Yes. The commission starts with the decisions and capabilities already in place. Design authority can stand on its own, or include me holding the technical seat through the first build.

items.question: What have you built?
answer: A new digital business next to an industrial parent, as its CTO. An AI agent now in production at an insurance brokerage. Two ventures of my own. The work page has the detail.

items.question: How does a commission start?
answer: With a thirty-minute conversation. Then we look at the options for the owner, including those with no venture in them, before anyone commits to a build.

cases.title: A new business, from the ground up.
cases.subtitle: A digital business next to an industrial parent
cases.summary: A digital business stood up alongside an industrial parent. One technical seat, held through the first build.
cases.context: During nine years at McKinsey, I served as CTO of North America's first large-scale digital business build. I was brought in for two weeks as product owner and stayed as CTO.
cases.design: I designed the new company's technology from scratch: its architecture, enterprise security posture, engineering environment and the boundary between the parent's legacy systems and the new company's stack.
cases.evidence: I have held the technical seat in a venture built next to a parent, and worked the boundary with the parent's CIO.
cases.visualCaption: Illustrative model of the boundary between a parent and a new venture.
cases.visualAlt: A new venture is connected to an industrial parent across a defined boundary.

cases.title: An agent that made it into production.
cases.subtitle: An AI agent for an insurance brokerage
cases.summary: An AI agent designed and built for an insurance brokerage. Technical choices grounded in an operating business.
cases.context: As an independent, I designed and built an AI agent for an insurance brokerage. The system is in production, and my work there is complete.
cases.design: I built the agent on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK and made the case for the model choice against an incumbent enterprise agreement.
cases.evidence: The model choice was a business decision as well as a technical one. I carried that decision with executives and built the resulting system.
cases.visualCaption: Conceptual workflow illustration. It does not disclose the client's system.
cases.visualAlt: A conceptual agent workflow connects input, an AI system, human review and an outcome.

cases.title: The built environment, made measurable.

cases.summary: Aerial reality capture for the built environment, serving customers across the Midwest.
cases.context: Sightline Geospatial serves AEC firms, civil and county engineers, general contractors, utilities and aggregate producers across the Midwest.
cases.design: I chose the market, the unit and the price for an aerial reality capture business. I operate the venture and answer for its margin.
cases.evidence: I live with my own design decisions. The relationship between an offer, its delivery and its economics is part of the daily work.

cases.title: A small component. A larger system.
cases.subtitle: Miniature Systems

cases.context: Miniature Systems makes payload accessories for uncrewed aircraft. The venture serves a market shaped by the requirements of a larger platform and a regulated buyer.
cases.design: The work centers on the relationship between the accessory and the platform it depends on: what it adds, what it inherits and where the boundary belongs.
cases.evidence: In a hardware venture, inherited constraints are part of the business design. I make those choices in a venture of my own.

seo.description: Architect of applications, then of enterprises, then of ventures. A founder, photographer and independent venture architect based in Iowa City.

hero.title: Same noun. Bigger object.
hero.body: Architect of applications, then of enterprises, then of ventures.

opening.title: I have been an architect of one kind or another for more than a decade.
paragraphs: First of applications, as a lead architect at Appirio. Then of the front-office systems of large enterprises, during nine years at McKinsey. Now of whole ventures.
The object has changed. The work still asks the same question: how do the parts fit, and who is accountable for the whole?

items.title: Applications
items.label: Appirio
items.body: Two years as a lead architect, designing applications and the systems around them.

items.title: Enterprises
items.label: McKinsey
items.body: Nine years on the expert path, in the guild for software, cloud, cyber and architecture, working on the front-office systems of large enterprises.

items.title: Ventures
items.label: Venture CTO and founder
items.body: CTO of a new digital business next to an industrial parent. Now designing AI-native ventures and running Sightline Geospatial and Miniature Systems.

technicalSeat.title: I went in for two weeks. I stayed as CTO.
paragraphs: At McKinsey, the work that shaped me most was serving as CTO of North America's first large-scale digital business build: a new company stood up from scratch next to an industrial parent.
I also spent two years as lead faculty for the firm's experienced-hire program. That taught me that a design is only finished when someone else can run it.

photographer.title: I still think in pictures.
paragraphs: Alongside the rest of my work, I spent fifteen years as a professional photographer. Looking closely, finding the relationship between things and deciding what to leave out are still part of how I design.
Before McKinsey, I co-founded a media company that filmed independent bands and a furniture importer where I built the commerce, service and supply chain systems myself.

today.title: Building on my own account.
paragraphs: I run Sightline Geospatial and Miniature Systems from Iowa City. One captures the built environment. The other makes NDAA-compliant payload accessories for uncrewed aircraft.
I have built AI systems hands-on since 2021. Most recently, I designed and built an agent for an insurance brokerage that is now in production.
I take a small number of commissions each year as venture architect for sponsors and founders, working from a written method of my own.
